title: The Séance
logline: Seven years after his death, a seance summons the founder of Pakistan, and he sees 'flashes of evil pictures'. Episode 1 of a ten-part documentary on Venkat Dhulipala's Creating a New Medina: the claim that Pakistan was not a vague accident but a plentifully imagined Islamic state, a new Medina, argued over in the towns of north India, and the critics who disagree.
note: Discusses the partition of India and its mass violence, and historical rhetoric about minorities. No graphic imagery.
source: Venkat Dhulipala, Creating a New Medina: State Power, Islam, and the Quest for Pakistan in Late Colonial North India (Cambridge University Press, 2015); reviews by F. Devji (The Wire, 2015), S. I. Khan (Marginalia Review), P. B. Mehta (Indian Express, 2015), I. Talbot (JAS, 2015); A. Jalal, The Sole Spokesman (1985).

title: The Broken Coalition
logline: In 1936 a small-town paper called the Muslim League 'neither dead nor alive'. Episode 2 goes back to the 1937 elections in the United Provinces, when Congress and the League were allies against the landlords, a Deobandi cleric campaigned for Jinnah, and nobody could yet say who was a nationalist and who a communalist.
note: Discusses the partition of India, communal politics and historical rhetoric about minorities. No graphic imagery.
source: Venkat Dhulipala, Creating a New Medina: State Power, Islam, and the Quest for Pakistan in Late Colonial North India (Cambridge University Press, 2015), chapter 1; Linlithgow and Haig papers, Venkatachar memoirs and the U.P. press as quoted there; Jalal and Seal (1981).

title: Four-Anna Members
logline: Shut out of power in 1937, the Muslim League took on Nehru's campaign to win Muslims with economics. Episode 3 follows the by-elections, the war over flags, songs and schools, a Sufi scholar's telegram and a bald parrot from Rumi, as a party 'neither dead nor alive' became a mass movement.
note: Discusses the partition of India, communal politics and historical rhetoric about minorities. No graphic imagery.
source: Venkat Dhulipala, Creating a New Medina: State Power, Islam, and the Quest for Pakistan in Late Colonial North India (Cambridge University Press, 2015), chapter 2; AICC Papers, the Hindustan weekly, Thanawi's collected opinions and governors' letters as quoted there.

title: Two Lawyers from Bombay
logline: In 1944 Jinnah told Gandhi to read a book on Pakistan written by Dr B. R. Ambedkar. Episode 4 follows the public argument that gave the Pakistan demand its maps, numbers and hostages, the League's answer, the failed talks on Malabar Hill, and the case against the idea that Pakistan was only a bargaining counter.
note: Discusses the partition of India, communal politics and historical rhetoric about minorities. No graphic imagery.
source: Venkat Dhulipala, Creating a New Medina: State Power, Islam, and the Quest for Pakistan in Late Colonial North India (Cambridge University Press, 2015), chapter 3; Ambedkar's Thoughts on Pakistan, MRT's volumes, the Gandhi-Jinnah correspondence and Jinnah's speeches as quoted there; Jalal (1985).

title: The Ideal Goal
logline: After the Lahore Resolution, the Muslim League's leaders in the United Provinces had to explain Pakistan to Muslims who would never live in it. Episode 5 follows the pamphlets, speeches and private letters: an Islamic state, a 'laboratory', a jumping-off ground for the Muslim world, a quiet readiness to accept a smaller Pakistan, and minorities held as hostages.
note: Discusses the partition of India, communal politics and historical rhetoric about minorities. No graphic imagery.
source: Venkat Dhulipala, Creating a New Medina: State Power, Islam, and the Quest for Pakistan in Late Colonial North India (Cambridge University Press, 2015), chapter 4; the pamphlets, speeches and archival letters quoted there.

title: The Other Medina
logline: Some of Pakistan's most determined Muslim opponents were men of religion. Episode 6 follows three critiques from the Deobandi camp and its allies: Sajjad's 'fraud of Islamic Pakistan', Manglori's sums for the Muslims left behind, and Seoharvi's warning that Islam would shrink into geography, plus the ulama's own plan for a united India.
note: Discusses the partition of India, communal politics and historical rhetoric about minorities. No graphic imagery.
source: Venkat Dhulipala, Creating a New Medina: State Power, Islam, and the Quest for Pakistan in Late Colonial North India (Cambridge University Press, 2015), chapter 5; the Urdu tracts and articles quoted there; Metcalf (2009) on Madani.

title: Letters to Madina
logline: In 1942 a pro-Congress Urdu paper in the small town of Bijnor asked its readers what they understood by Pakistan, and printed the answers. Episode 7 follows that debate: a critic who said mass migration was impossible, a defender who promised hostages on both sides, readers from Bombay to Raichur, and letters to Jinnah asking what Pakistan would mean for those left behind.
note: Discusses the partition of India, communal politics and historical rhetoric about minorities. No graphic imagery.
source: Venkat Dhulipala, Creating a New Medina: State Power, Islam, and the Quest for Pakistan in Late Colonial North India (Cambridge University Press, 2015), chapter 6; the Madina debate and letters in the Quaid-i-Azam Papers as quoted there.

title: The Shaikhul Islam
logline: Not all the Deobandi ulama stood with Congress. Episode 8 follows Shabbir Ahmad Usmani, who broke with his colleagues, founded a pro-League party of scholars, and sold Pakistan to voters as the new Medina, with Jinnah as the ship's English captain and the ulama as its pilots.
note: Discusses the partition of India, communal politics and historical rhetoric about minorities. No graphic imagery.
source: Venkat Dhulipala, Creating a New Medina: State Power, Islam, and the Quest for Pakistan in Late Colonial North India (Cambridge University Press, 2015), chapter 7; Usmani's speeches and the account of the 1945 Deoband meeting as quoted there.

title: The Referendum
logline: The elections of 1945 and 1946 become a referendum on Pakistan. Episode 9 follows a divided League, Aligarh's pamphlets and student foot soldiers, the songs, the cap auctioned for sixteen thousand rupees, Madani and Nehru's counter-campaign, and the result: two in three U.P. Muslim voters back a country they will never live in.
note: Discusses the partition of India, communal politics and historical rhetoric about minorities. No graphic imagery.
source: Venkat Dhulipala, Creating a New Medina: State Power, Islam, and the Quest for Pakistan in Late Colonial North India (Cambridge University Press, 2015), chapter 8; party papers, pamphlets, poems and the 1946 OSS report as quoted there.

title: Rivers of Blood, and After
logline: The final episode. Partition comes to U.P.: the leaders leave, the Muslims who stay are asked to prove their loyalty, and Pakistan's founders argue over what their new Medina should be. From a Karachi funeral to a Raja's exile to a mohajir leader's apology in Delhi in 2004, and the series' verdict on the book.
note: Discusses the partition of India, communal politics and historical rhetoric about minorities. No graphic imagery.
source: Venkat Dhulipala, Creating a New Medina: State Power, Islam, and the Quest for Pakistan in Late Colonial North India (Cambridge University Press, 2015), epilogue and conclusion; official reports, memoirs and newspapers as quoted there.

title: Eight Nights of Fire
logline: In June 2023 a police officer shot 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk in Nanterre, and France burned for eight nights. A sourced, illustrated account of the riots: the damage, the attacks on police, mayors and town halls, the phones that spread it, the second riot online, who the rioters were, and whether Gad Saad's 'suicidal empathy', especially his claim about women, holds up against the data.
note: Adult audiences: describes riot violence, arson, a death and online hate factually. Stylised imagery, no graphic content.
source: French Senate inquiry (April 2024); Interior Ministry (G. Darmanin, July 2023); Justice Ministry (E. Dupond-Moretti, Aug 2023); France Assureurs (March 2024); Ifop polls for Le Figaro (29-30 June) and Sud Radio (4-5 July 2023); EDMO and Logically fact-checks; Reuters, AFP, NPR, The Local; Cour de cassation (12 June 2026). Framing from 'Suicidal Empathy' by Gad Saad (2026), paraphrased and attributed, with counterpoints.

title: Who Burned France?
logline: A school strike over crowded classrooms became France's worst riots in years on 17 October 2026. A mapped, sourced account of what burned, who was arrested, what Asra Nomani's 'Chaos Inc.' investigation found, and whether the viral claim that immigrants used the student protests as cover holds up.
note: Adult audiences: describes riot violence, arson, injuries to children and police, and online hate factually. Stylised imagery, no graphic content.
source: Interior Ministry (L. Nuñez) and Justice Ministry (G. Darmanin), Oct 2026; PM S. Lecornu; Limoges prefecture; Asra Q. Nomani, Fox News Digital (9 and 20 Oct 2026); AP Fact Focus (20 Oct); NewsGuard; The Week fact check; Reuters, AP, AFP, Al Jazeera, Le Figaro, Sud Radio, actu17, Wikipedia timeline. Figures as of 23 October 2026.

title: Four Nights
logline: Late August. In a 24-hour coin laundry by the canal, a teasing seventeen-year-old notices that the silent man at the far end of the bench is reading her late grandfather's favourite story, about a lonely dreamer who gets four nights with a girl on a bridge.
category: Dostoevsky at the Coin Laundry (anime series)
source: Original story. Discusses White Nights (1848); Dostoevsky passages are our own renderings of the public-domain texts.

title: Two Times Two Makes Five
logline: Early September. Mio has read "Notes from Underground" all week to understand the silent man from the laundry, and has a new name for him. They argue about spite, freedom and the man who spent years planning to bump into an officer, and both admit what keeps them underground.
category: Dostoevsky at the Coin Laundry (anime series)
source: Original story. Discusses Notes from Underground (1864); Dostoevsky passages are our own renderings of the public-domain texts.

title: Letters in the Lost-and-Found
logline: Late September. For the first time, Mio isn't there when Itsuki arrives. She has left him a letter in the laundry's lost-and-found notebook, because Dostoevsky's first novel is made of letters, and because some things are easier to say on paper. He writes back.
category: Dostoevsky at the Coin Laundry (anime series)
source: Original story. Discusses Poor Folk (1846); Dostoevsky passages are our own renderings of the public-domain texts.

title: The Idea with an Axe
logline: October, and a typhoon. Mio has been carrying an ugly thought about the baby for a week. Over Raskolnikov and the theory that carried him to murder, Itsuki admits the theory he once used on himself, and when the power fails, Mio says her thought out loud in the dark.
category: Dostoevsky at the Coin Laundry (anime series)
source: Original story. Discusses Crime and Punishment (1866); Dostoevsky passages are our own renderings of the public-domain texts.

title: Somewhere to Go
logline: Late October. Mio arrives with yellow paint on her fingers, ready to argue about Marmeladov, the drunk who asks whether a man has somewhere to go. Then Itsuki's phone rings, and it's his mother, who calls him by his father's name. Mio sits with him in silence. And Mrs. Hoshino has news about the laundry.
category: Dostoevsky at the Coin Laundry (anime series)
source: Original story. Discusses Crime and Punishment (1866); Dostoevsky passages are our own renderings of the public-domain texts.

title: The Prince of the Coin Laundry
logline: November. A drunk salaryman who has missed the last train is asleep on the laundry bench, and Mio doesn't know what to do. Itsuki does. Watching him, she understands Dostoevsky's attempt to write a perfectly good man, and gives Itsuki the name that will stick. On the way out, he buys her a hot milk tea without asking.
category: Dostoevsky at the Coin Laundry (anime series)
source: Original story. Discusses The Idiot (1869); Dostoevsky passages are our own renderings of the public-domain texts.

title: Money in the Fire
logline: Late November. A classmate has seen Mio at the laundry with "an old guy," and the gossip has followed her all week. Over Nastasya Filippovna, who throws a hundred thousand roubles into the fire, and proud Aglaya, who mocks the prince because she loves him, Mio says one sentence too many. Itsuki answers with the most careful thing he can think of, and they have their first quarrel.
category: Dostoevsky at the Coin Laundry (anime series)
source: Original story. Discusses The Idiot (1869); Dostoevsky passages are our own renderings of the public-domain texts.

title: Twenty-Six Days
logline: Early December and the first snow. Mio has found, in the city library, a five-year-old literary magazine with Itsuki's photograph in it. Over the novel Dostoevsky dictated in twenty-six days to save everything he had written, and the morning he stood in front of a firing squad, she offers him a deal: one page, every Thursday, until the laundry closes.
category: Dostoevsky at the Coin Laundry (anime series)
source: Original story. Discusses The Gambler (1866); Dostoevsky passages are our own renderings of the public-domain texts.

title: The Ridiculous Man
logline: Mid-December. Mio's mother has gone into hospital three weeks early, and for two Thursdays the bench is empty. Alone with Dostoevsky's strangest short story, about a man who had decided nothing mattered until a little girl in the rain proved him wrong, Itsuki remembers the winter he wanted nothing, and keeps the notebook company until she comes back.
category: Dostoevsky at the Coin Laundry (anime series)
source: Original story. Discusses The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877); Dostoevsky passages are our own renderings of the public-domain texts.

title: Returning the Ticket
logline: January, deep snow. Mio announces, very casually, that she won't apply to the university in Tokyo after all: her mother needs help with the baby, and the local college is fine. Over Ivan Karamazov's rebellion and his poem of the Grand Inquisitor, who takes away people's freedom to make them comfortable, Itsuki argues for her freedom against his own heart, and tells her to go.
category: Dostoevsky at the Coin Laundry (anime series)
source: Original story. Discusses The Brothers Karamazov (1880); Dostoevsky passages are our own renderings of the public-domain texts.

title: Forgiveness of the Birds
logline: February. On the same Saturday, Mio takes the train to Tokyo for her entrance exam and Itsuki takes the local line to his mother's care home, carrying Father Zosima's story of his dying brother, who asked the birds to forgive him. That Thursday, Mrs. Hoshino tells Mio something about Itsuki's washing machine that he will never say himself.
category: Dostoevsky at the Coin Laundry (anime series)
source: Original story. Discusses The Brothers Karamazov (1880); Dostoevsky passages are our own renderings of the public-domain texts.

title: Let Us Never Forget One Another
logline: Late March, the last night of the Coin Laundry Hoshizora, and the thirty-first Thursday. Mio leaves for Tokyo on Saturday. Over the last chapter of Dostoevsky's last novel, Alyosha's speech to twelve schoolboys at a stone, the two of them give each other the only presents that fit, and Itsuki finally fixes the sign.
category: Dostoevsky at the Coin Laundry (anime series)
source: Original story. Discusses The Brothers Karamazov (1880); Dostoevsky passages are our own renderings of the public-domain texts.

title: Demons: The Revolution That Ate Its Own
logline: A paper-collage video essay on Dostoevsky's Demons: the real 1869 murder behind it, the liberal fathers and nihilist sons, Shigalyov's paradise for one tenth, the fashionable people who flattered the radicals, three kinds of freedom, and the strongest case against Dostoevsky's verdict on the revolutionary left.
note: Describes murders, a suicide and political violence from the novel and from history. A crime against a child is named but not described. Stylised paper-collage imagery, nothing graphic.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, Demons (1871-72), Garnett translation (1916); Joseph Frank; Philip Pomper; Franco Venturi; Catechism of a Revolutionary (1869); Berdyaev (1918); Camus (1959); Gorky (1913).

title: Dying to Be Kind
logline: When Mayor Hart cranks the town's Empathy Dial to eleven, Penny Doormat has to save her spineless dad, his credit score and the whole damn town by working out when kindness helps and when it gets you robbed by a raccoon.
source: Ideas from 'Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind' by Gad Saad (2026), plus published criticism of the book (The Bulwark, Quillette).

title: Dying to Be Kind (Family Cut)
logline: When Mayor Hart cranks the town's Empathy Dial to eleven, Penny Doormat has to save her too-nice dad, her fridge and her whole town by learning when kindness helps and when it backfires.
source: Ideas from 'Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind' by Gad Saad (2026), plus published criticism of the book (The Bulwark, Quillette).

title: Justice-Involved Raccoon
logline: When Kindleton bans hurtful facts and renames every crime, Penny's science fair project gets cancelled for being true, and Dale gets convicted by the internet for a crime nobody can name.
source: Ideas from 'Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind' by Gad Saad (2026), plus published criticism of the book (The Bulwark, Quillette).

title: Hairworm Season
logline: Kindleton assumes its brutal softball rivals secretly want participation trophies too, and Dale starts cheering for the other team so hard he jumps in the town fountain.
source: Ideas from 'Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind' by Gad Saad (2026), plus published criticism of the book (The Bulwark, Quillette).

title: Blank Slate Felons
logline: Kindleton's bike thief walks free for the forty-first time, while Dale stops a robbery and gets sentenced to Masculinity Unlearning.
source: Ideas from 'Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind' by Gad Saad (2026), plus published criticism of the book (The Bulwark, Quillette).

title: The Settled Science Fair
logline: Kindleton declares all science settled, locks itself indoors over one sneeze and bans exhaling, until Penny builds a booth with a big red button that says Prove Me Wrong.
source: Ideas from 'Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind' by Gad Saad (2026), plus published criticism of the book (The Bulwark, Quillette).

title: Indulgence Inc.
logline: Brightside MegaCorp starts selling Guilt Offsets, the hospital hires a surgeon for his energy, and Dale loses three organs to good vibes.
source: Ideas from 'Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind' by Gad Saad (2026), plus published criticism of the book (The Bulwark, Quillette).

title: Govern Me Harder, Daddy!
logline: Mayor Hart makes everything in Kindleton free and taxes everyone at one hundred and ten percent, and Penny's lemonade stand goes bankrupt in one afternoon.
source: Ideas from 'Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind' by Gad Saad (2026), plus published criticism of the book (The Bulwark, Quillette).

title: Dial M for Moderation
logline: Season finale. The Empathy Dial goes on trial for crimes against common sense, with Penny prosecuting, the Mayor defending, and Rocco as the key witness.
source: Ideas from 'Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind' by Gad Saad (2026), plus published criticism of the book (The Bulwark, Quillette).

title: Too Kind to Survive?
logline: Can a society care itself to death? A calm, illustrated tour of Gad Saad's 'Suicidal Empathy': where empathy comes from, how it misfires, why it feels so good, what his critics say, and the habits worth keeping either way.
source: Ideas from 'Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind' by Gad Saad (2026), paraphrased, with published criticism (The Bulwark, Quillette). Also cited: Randolph Nesse on emotions, Robert Axelrod's tit-for-tat tournaments, Thomas Sowell and Rob Henderson on luxury beliefs.

title: The Things We Won’t Say
logline: Should a fact ever be hidden to spare feelings? Chapter 2 of Gad Saad's 'Suicidal Empathy' on forbidden knowledge, softened words, compassion without conditions, and the fable of the scorpion, with the strongest counterpoints.
source: Chapter 2 ('Forbidden Knowledge') of 'Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind' by Gad Saad (2026), paraphrased. Public record: Fryer (2016); Harvard (2019); US DHS (2022); reporting on the 2018 Tajikistan attack.

title: Same Species, Different Rules
logline: Are all cultures equal? Chapter 3 of Gad Saad's 'Suicidal Empathy' on the 'cultural theory of mind', harmful practices, Canada's postnational idea, England's grooming gang scandal and uneven empathy, with the strongest counterpoints.
note: Discusses child sexual exploitation, FGM and honour killings factually, without graphic detail.
source: Chapter 3 ('Cultural Theory of Mind') of 'Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind' by Gad Saad (2026), paraphrased. Public record: Jay Report (2014), Casey Audit (2025), UNICEF (2024), ADL (2023).

title: Second Chances
logline: Can compassion for offenders cost victims? Chapter 4 of Gad Saad's 'Suicidal Empathy' on repeat offenders, defunding the police, the Penny case, 'sneaky' signalling and lenient courts, with the strongest counterpoints. For adults.
note: Adult audiences: discusses rape and murder factually, and one crude zoology nickname. No graphic content.
source: Chapter 4 ('Blank Slate Felons') of 'Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind' by Gad Saad (2026), paraphrased. Public record: BJS recidivism study (2021); Penny trial (2024); Freiburg trial (2018).

title: Settled?
logline: When does 'settled science' stop being science? Chapter 5 of Gad Saad's 'Suicidal Empathy' on Semmelweis, falsifiability, taboo trade-offs, COVID policy, climate anxiety and youth gender medicine, with the strongest counterpoints.
source: Chapter 5 ('Settled Science, Taboo Trade-Offs') of 'Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind' by Gad Saad (2026), paraphrased. Public record: Cass Review (2024); New York Times (2024); Ioannidis et al. (2023); Watson et al. (2022).

title: Buying Absolution
logline: Is DEI a modern indulgence? Chapter 6 of Gad Saad's 'Suicidal Empathy' on opportunity versus outcome, diversity statements, dropped tests, hiring in medicine and safety, and brand backlash, with the strongest counterpoints.
source: Chapter 6 ('Selling Indulgences') of 'Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind' by Gad Saad (2026), paraphrased. Public record: university test-policy announcements (2024); FAA litigation; AB InBev results (2023).

title: The Kindest Government
logline: Does the welfare state run on empathy? Chapter 7 of Gad Saad's 'Suicidal Empathy' on ants and socialism, New Harmony, taxation, Canada's healthcare waits, the nanny state and the military, with the strongest counterpoints. Series finale.
source: Chapter 7 ('Govern Me Harder, Daddy!') of 'Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind' by Gad Saad (2026), paraphrased. Public record: Fraser Institute (2023); Quebec and federal tax tables (2022).

title: The Red-Green Alliance
logline: Is there a 'Red-Green Alliance' of the hard left and Islamists? A sourced investigation of Asra Nomani's case, stamping every claim as on the record, her reporting, her analysis, or disputed.
note: Discusses terrorism financing cases, political violence in Iran and contested political labels, factually and without graphic imagery.
source: Asra Q. Nomani, Woke Army (2023) and Fox News (2025-26); US v. Holy Land Foundation; UAE, Texas and US designations; US Education Dept; New York Times; House Ways and Means; Pew Research Center; CNRS. Figures as of 23 October 2026.

title: Who Burned France? Revised Cut
logline: The revised cut of LUMEN's October 2026 riots special. Blunter about the ultra-left violence, the Palestinian flags in the riots, the State's own report on Islamist entryism, Islam's measured growth in France, and the politicians and influencers who excused the damage, while still testing every claim against the record.
note: Adult audiences: describes riot violence, arson, injuries to children and police, Islamist entryism and online hate factually. Stylised imagery, no graphic content.
source: Interior Ministry (L. Nuñez) and Justice Ministry (G. Darmanin), Oct 2026; PM S. Lecornu; Limoges prefecture; Asra Q. Nomani, Fox News Digital (9 and 20 Oct 2026); AP Fact Focus (20 Oct); NewsGuard; The Week fact check; Reuters, AP, AFP, Al Jazeera, Le Figaro, Sud Radio, actu17, Wikipedia timeline. Figures as of 23 October 2026. Revised cut adds: INSEE TeO2 (2023); 'Frères musulmans et islamisme politique en France' report (May 2025, via Public Sénat); Ifop for Écran de veille (Nov 2025) and the CDCM complaint against it; L'Appel (20 Oct 2026); Sud Radio (27 Feb 2025); LCI via Le Tribunal du Net, i24NEWS and Townhall (20-21 Oct 2026); Le Tribunal du Net (18 Oct 2026); ICI Isère.

source: महागाथा: पुराणों की 100 कथाएँ, सत्यार्थ नायक, हिंदी अनुवाद आशुतोष गर्ग

title: शक्ति (Shakti)
logline: हल्दी से गढ़ा एक बालक जो महादेव का मार्ग रोक देता है, सब देवताओं के तेज से जन्मी दुर्गा और महिषासुर का नौ दिन का युद्ध, और वह असुर जिसके रक्त की हर बूँद नया असुर बन जाती थी। (Hindi, pichwai style)
source: महागाथा: पुराणों की 100 कथाएँ, सत्यार्थ नायक, हिंदी अनुवाद आशुतोष गर्ग

title: तीन पग (Three Steps)
logline: एक राजा जिसे एक गाय ने ऋषि बना दिया, एक राजकुमार जो स्वर्ग और धरती के बीच उल्टा लटक गया, और एक नन्हा ब्राह्मण जिसने तीन पग में तीनों लोक नाप लिए। (Hindi, pichwai style)
source: महागाथा: पुराणों की 100 कथाएँ, सत्यार्थ नायक, हिंदी अनुवाद आशुतोष गर्ग

title: गंगावतरण (Descent of the Ganga)
logline: विष के साथ जन्मा राजा, राख बने साठ हज़ार पुत्र, चार पीढ़ियों का तप, शिव की जटा में समाई गंगा, और फरसे वाला वह ब्राह्मण जिसने इक्कीस बार धरती को अत्याचारी राजाओं से मुक्त किया। (Hindi, pichwai style)
source: महागाथा: पुराणों की 100 कथाएँ, सत्यार्थ नायक, हिंदी अनुवाद आशुतोष गर्ग

title: लंका (Lanka)
logline: सोने की नगरी जो एक भाई ने दूसरे से छीन ली, दस सिर काटकर माँगा गया शिवलिंग और देवताओं की एक शरारत, सीता के चार शाप, और वह छाया जिसे रावण कभी पहचान नहीं पाया। (Hindi, pichwai style)
source: महागाथा: पुराणों की 100 कथाएँ, सत्यार्थ नायक, हिंदी अनुवाद आशुतोष गर्ग

title: कान्हा (Kanha)
logline: मथुरा का कारागार, एक बरसती रात में यमुना पार करती टोकरी, आठ भुजाओं वाली योगमाया की चेतावनी, विषैले नाग के फन पर नाचता बालक, और छोटी अँगुली पर उठा एक पूरा पर्वत। (Hindi, pichwai style)
source: महागाथा: पुराणों की 100 कथाएँ, सत्यार्थ नायक, हिंदी अनुवाद आशुतोष गर्ग

title: ऋण (The Debt (Finale))
logline: मुट्ठी भर चावल का ऋण, जो एक राजा दस गुना लौटाता है। लोहे के नरकट, जो एक पूरे वंश को निगल जाते हैं। एक शिकारी का बाण, जो युगों पुराना हिसाब चुकाता है। और एक यज्ञ, जिसमें संसार के सारे सर्प जलने वाले थे, जब तक एक बालक ने गाना नहीं शुरू किया। (Hindi, pichwai style)
source: महागाथा: पुराणों की 100 कथाएँ, सत्यार्थ नायक, हिंदी अनुवाद आशुतोष गर्ग

title: The Pillar of Fire
logline: Brahma and Vishnu go to war over who is supreme, until a column of fire with no beginning and no end splits the sky between them.
source: Shiva Purana, Vidyeshvara Samhita, chapters 6 to 9 (tr. Bibek Debroy)

hi.label: हिंदी
hi.title: अग्नि-स्तंभ
hi.logline: ब्रह्मा और विष्णु में श्रेष्ठता को लेकर युद्ध छिड़ जाता है, तभी उनके बीच एक ऐसा अग्नि-स्तंभ प्रकट होता है जिसका न आदि है न अंत।

title: Narada's Pride
logline: Narada defeats desire, and then boasts about it. So Vishnu builds him a city, a princess and a very surprising face.
source: Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita, Srishti Khanda, chapters 2 to 4 (tr. Bibek Debroy)

hi.label: हिंदी
hi.title: नारद का अभिमान
hi.logline: नारद काम को जीत लेते हैं, और फिर उसका बखान करते हैं। तब विष्णु उनके लिए एक नगर, एक राजकुमारी और एक बड़ा अनोखा चेहरा रचते हैं।

title: The Thief and the Lamp
logline: A gambler steals food from a temple on Shivaratri and tears his cloth to brighten a lamp. That one flame carries him across three lives, all the way to Kailasa.
source: Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita, Srishti Khanda, chapters 17 to 19 (tr. Bibek Debroy)

hi.label: हिंदी
hi.title: चोर और दीपक
hi.logline: एक जुआरी शिवरात्रि पर मंदिर से भोग चुराता है और दीपक तेज़ करने के लिए अपना वस्त्र फाड़ देता है। वही एक लौ उसे तीन जन्मों के पार, कैलास तक ले जाती है।

title: Chanchula
logline: A woman who wasted her life hears a few words of Shiva's story and turns around. Then she goes back for the husband who became a ghost.
source: Shiva Purana, Shiva Purana Mahatmya, chapters 3 to 5 (tr. Bibek Debroy)
